To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
saccade latencies are increased when hand movements and saccades aim at opposite directions.
the preparation for a saccade is modulated by the preparation for a concomitant hand movement.

hand movements affect both behavioral and electrophysiologic parameters of saccadic eye movements, particularly if the movements are in the same direction as the eye movement, and if both movements are directed towards a common visual stimulus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of saccade and hand movement preparation and its neural correlates in healthy subjects.
the question of how the brain processes the information that is necessary to coordinate the movements of two effectors, the eye and the hand, in space and time.
the question of whether the motor system is a modular or a unitary system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hand movements in the opposite direction interfere with saccadic latencies but not with saccade-related brain potentials.

the saccade preparation system has access to information about the preparation of hand movements in the direction of saccade execution and that it is affected by hand movements that are prepared simultaneously.
the hand movement preparation interferes with the saccade preparation in a direction-specific manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
saccades to the right are faster than saccades to left, and that saccades with the hand moving in the opposite direction are slower than saccades with no hand movements.
hand movements influence saccade preparation and that this influence depends on the direction of the two movements.
saccade-related brain activity can be modulated by the concurrent preparation of a hand movement, but only when the two motor programs share a common sensory input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the saccade preparation process is affected by hand movements, particularly when they are in the same direction.
saccade-related brain activity is modulated by the direction of hand movement.
hand movements interfere with oculomotor behavior, particularly when both movements are in the same direction and thus access the same visual stimuli.
